title: Congress Started Asking for Trump's Exit Plan Because He Took the Country to War Without One
description_short: Congress Started Asking for Trump's Exit Plan Because He Took the Country to War Without One
description_medium: On March 21, 2026, members of Congress sought the administration’s plan for ending the Iran war, according to the linked AP headline. The packet frames their questions around the war’s objectives and Congress’s role in authorizing force, but supplies no lawmakers’ names, requested benchmarks or administration response.

preserved_fields.title: Congress Started Asking for Trump's Exit Plan Because He Took the Country to War Without One
preserved_fields.description_short: Congress Started Asking for Trump's Exit Plan Because He Took the Country to War Without One

notes: The linked AP page returned HTTP 403 in the focused read. The headline and packet show that Congress sought an exit plan, but provide no members, specific questions, proposed benchmarks or administration answer. The claim that Trump had no plan is not established by the headline alone.
proposed_correction: Congress Seeks Trump's Plan for Ending the Iran War

title: Trump's Deportation Machine Was Sending Parents Away Without Their Children
description_short: Trump's Deportation Machine Was Sending Parents Away Without Their Children
description_medium: A report cited by The Guardian found that many parents deported to Honduras were not asked whether they had children or given a chance to arrange care before removal. Researchers interviewed dozens of deported parents, health professionals, government officials and reception-center staff. The report said the practice appeared to violate the administration’s own policies.
description_long: The Guardian reported on March 19, 2026, that a study found the Trump administration was deporting parents without asking whether they had children or allowing them to decide whether their children would travel with them. Researchers interviewed dozens of parents deported to Honduras, along with physicians, psychologists, government officials and staff at deportee reception centers. They found that many parents were removed soon after detention without time to arrange care for children left behind. The report said the practice appeared to violate the administration’s own policies. The article described family separation through deportation procedures: in some cases, children remained in the United States while a parent was sent to Honduras. It did not establish that officials intended to traumatize families, and its findings do not describe every deportation case. The report documents a gap between written procedures and the experiences parents recounted, raising questions about how consistently agencies identified children and handled family-care arrangements before removal.

preserved_fields.title: Trump's Deportation Machine Was Sending Parents Away Without Their Children
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's Deportation Machine Was Sending Parents Away Without Their Children

notes: The linked Guardian report was read directly. It supports interviews with dozens of parents deported to Honduras and reports that many had no chance to arrange care; the description removes the prior claim of intentional trauma.

title: Trump Told Allies to Handle Hormuz Themselves While Still Refusing to Leave
description_short: Trump Told Allies to Handle Hormuz Themselves While Still Refusing to Leave
description_medium: On March 31, 2026, Trump said the United States was not ready to withdraw from efforts around the Strait of Hormuz, while telling allies they needed to “come in and take care of it.” He criticized countries that had not sent military assets and said the strait posed no substantial threat despite continuing Iranian attacks on ships and regional infrastructure.
description_long: In a March 31, 2026, interview with CBS News, Donald Trump said he was not ready “quite yet” to remove U.S. assets from efforts to force Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. He also said other countries had to “come in and take care of it,” criticizing allies, including the United Kingdom, for not sending military assets to join the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran. Trump argued that countries needing oil should secure it themselves and said the strait posed “no real threat” despite ongoing Iranian strikes on ships and infrastructure in Persian Gulf countries. The waterway is a major oil transit route, carrying about one-fifth of the world’s supply, according to CBS. His remarks paired continued U.S. involvement with a demand that allies assume more responsibility. The interview records his position at that time; it does not report that the United States had withdrawn or that allies had taken over protection of the route.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Told Allies to Handle Hormuz Themselves While Still Refusing to Leave
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Told Allies to Handle Hormuz Themselves While Still Refusing to Leave

notes: The linked CBS report was read directly. It supports Trump’s simultaneous statements about continued U.S. involvement and allied responsibility, as well as his assessment of the risk to shipping. The description does not infer his motive.

title: Trump Moved the Forest Service Out of Washington in Another Attack on Scientists Who Wouldn't Play Along
description_short: Trump Moved the Forest Service Out of Washington in Another Attack on Scientists Who Wouldn't Play Along
description_medium: The Trump administration announced that the U.S. Forest Service headquarters would move from Washington, D.C., to Salt Lake City and that the agency’s regional offices would close. USDA called it a reorganization; critics described it as an attack on science. The announcement does not show that particular scientists were targeted or that the move was completed.
description_long: The Guardian reported on March 31, 2026, that the Agriculture Department planned to move the U.S. Forest Service headquarters from Washington, D.C., to Salt Lake City and close its regional offices. The announcement put into motion a reorganization officials had been planning since the prior year. USDA described the move as a “commonsense approach,” while critics called it an attack on science and scientists. The report compared it with the first Trump administration’s relocation of the Bureau of Land Management from Washington to Colorado. Nearly 90 percent of the BLM’s Washington-based staff declined to move, and the agency later returned to Washington under President Biden. That history helps explain concerns that relocation could disrupt staffing and institutional knowledge, but it does not establish how many Forest Service employees would leave or whether the same outcome would occur. The announcement described a planned headquarters move and regional-office closures; it did not say the change had already been completed or that scientists were being punished for refusing to support administration policy.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Moved the Forest Service Out of Washington in Another Attack on Scientists Who Wouldn't Play Along
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Moved the Forest Service Out of Washington in Another Attack on Scientists Who Wouldn't Play Along

notes: The linked Guardian report was read directly. It supports the planned headquarters move, regional-office closures and BLM comparison, but not the title’s claim that scientists were targeted for refusing to cooperate. Proposed correction removes the motive claim and distinguishes an announcement from completed relocation.
proposed_correction: Trump Administration Announces Forest Service Headquarters Move and Regional Office Closures

title: Trump Posted an AI Jesus Version of Himself and Then Tried to Slither Away From It
description_short: Trump Posted an AI Jesus Version of Himself and Then Tried to Slither Away From It
description_medium: The Guardian reported that Trump posted an AI-generated image depicting himself as a Jesus-like figure on Truth Social on April 12, 2026, then deleted it after criticism from conservative Christian supporters. That day, he also attacked Pope Leo XIV online. The report documents the posts and backlash, not the motive implied by the title.
description_long: The Guardian reported that Donald Trump posted an AI-generated image to Truth Social on April 12, 2026, showing him with light emanating from his hands as he appeared to heal a patient in a hospital bed. A demon-like figure appeared in the background. Trump deleted the image after criticism from some conservative Christian supporters, who called it “disgusting.” Earlier that day, he had posted a lengthy attack on Pope Leo XIV, calling him “weak on crime” and criticizing his views. Trump declined to apologize for the image and said he was responding to the pope. The report documents the image, its deletion, the public reaction and Trump’s explanation. It does not establish why he posted the image or that he was trying to evade responsibility afterward. The episode prompted a dispute over religious imagery and presidential conduct, but the supplied title’s phrase “slither away” is an editorial characterization rather than a reported action.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Posted an AI Jesus Version of Himself and Then Tried to Slither Away From It
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Posted an AI Jesus Version of Himself and Then Tried to Slither Away From It

notes: The linked Guardian report was read directly. It supports the image, deletion, reaction and Trump’s stated response to the pope, but not the title’s claim that he tried to evade responsibility. The category was missing, so Authoritarianism is used for this presidential self-presentation entry; the editorial title should be neutralized.
proposed_correction: Trump Deletes AI-Generated Jesus-Like Image After Criticism From Christian Supporters
